Using power responsibly

I can. May I? Should I?

“Can I?”, “May I?” and “Should I?” are three different questions.

A closer lookOpen in a larger view ↗

The interactive example has its own motion control. Scroll inside it if you need more room.

A philosophical and theological argument

Being able to do something is about capability. Having permission is about who can authorize it. Deciding whether to do it also means considering the situation and its consequences.

Open the three doors. The example is a message that could change someone’s plans. No message is sent; the doors help you examine the decision.

Open each door. Each asks a different question about the same proposed action.

Read the fuller explanation

Capability asks what an agent can bring about. Permission asks which actions are legitimate. Responsibility asks what the situation calls for among those possibilities. The kenotic synthesis separates these questions before developing its account of divine action.

The distinction also supplies an editorial question for machine delegation. A system may be able to generate a proposal, alter a record or carry out a plan. That ability alone cannot settle who should authorize the act or remain answerable for its consequences.

Notice where an interface makes these doors appear to be one door. A smooth path from suggestion to execution can conceal the moment at which another person’s judgment was needed. The design question is where to make that moment legible.

Where this comes from: Power, restraint and responsibility

Theological and philosophical argument

A philosophical and theological argument

Distinguishes the ability to use power from permission and responsibility. It makes room for both restraint and protection. It is not a scientific law.

Read the full source note

Kenotic governance and shared responsibility

Capability, moral permission and an obligation to exercise power are distinguished. Restraint must also be examined where one agent destroys another’s effective agency. The argument remains defeasible and is not a physical derivation.
